name: Building world models for prediction and planning
gist: Papers teaching robots to predict what will happen next in their environment and use those predictions to plan better actions—world models learn to simulate the physics of the scene.
explain: A robot that can predict the future is much more capable than one that can only react to the present. If a robot pushes a block and can predict that it will slide across the table and fall off the edge, it can decide not to push so hard. If a robot predicts that a person will step into a crosswalk, it can brake preemptively. These predictions require a model of the world—an internal simulation of physics. The robot learns from experience: it watches what happens when it takes actions, and it builds a model that says 'if I push with force F at angle Θ, the object will move in direction D.' With such a model, the robot can reason about future outcomes without actually trying them.

The difficulty is that the world is complex and physics is hard. Real friction varies with materials and temperature. Objects deform in complicated ways. Multiple objects interact—one block hits another and they both move. Liquids splash and flow. Hair tangles. Cloth wrinkles. Simulating all of this requires detailed knowledge of material properties and numerical stability. Also, the robot's model is always incomplete and approximate. It sees the world through limited sensors. It does not know the exact mass of an object or the coefficient of friction. So the model is inherently uncertain, and that uncertainty grows as you predict further into the future, because small mistakes compound when you apply them repeatedly step by step. Errors compound—a small mistake about where an object is now becomes a large mistake about where it will be in five seconds.

Papers build world models using learned physics simulators—neural networks that predict the next state given the current state and an action. Some train these models on real robot data and in simulation, then use them for planning: the robot imagines taking different actions and uses the model to predict which one will succeed. Some use world models for control: instead of learning a direct mapping from observation to action, the robot learns a model and a separate 'imagination' module that uses the model to think about future actions. Some combine world models with other components: perception (estimate current state), world model (predict future states), reward model (evaluate which state is best), and planning (search over actions to find one that leads to good future states), so that all parts work together to make decisions. The goal across all these approaches is to give the robot the ability to think ahead.

papers.contribution: MoLA achieves consistent gains in task success, temporal consistency, and generalization on simulated benchmarks and real-world robot manipulation tasks.

papers.title: Geometry-aware 4D Video Generation for Robot Manipulation
papers.contribution: Produces visually stable and spatially aligned video predictions that generalize well to novel camera viewpoints for robot manipulation.

papers.title: Structured 4D Latent Predictive Model for Robot Planning
papers.contribution: Generates futures with strong visual quality and substantially better 3D consistency and multi-view coherence vs sota video-based planners; achieves superior manipulation performance with robust generalization to novel conditions.

papers.title: DeepSight: Long-Horizon World Modeling via Latent States Prediction for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.contribution: Achieves state-of-the-art results on closed-loop Bench2drive benchmark with long-horizon world modeling.

papers.title: MVISTA-4D: View-Consistent 4D World Model with Test-Time Action Inference for Robotic Manipulation
papers.contribution: Strong performance on both 4D scene generation and downstream manipulation across three datasets with practical insights from ablations.
